system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 11 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2145-05-18 22:08:00 to 2145-05-29 15:33:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with cellulitis and new pressure ulcers on both feet, discovered after he noticed redness and raw skin while being unable to feel pain due to paraplegia. He had a prior allergic reaction to vancomycin in the ED, prompting a switch to linezolid, which led to clinical improvement. Wound care was initiated, and a scheduled nephrostomy tube exchange was performed without complications. His infection resolved, white blood cell count normalized, and back pain stabilized. He was discharged home with instructions to complete a 10-day course of linezolid, continue protective foot care with waffle boots, and follow up with urology, nephrology, and plastic surgery.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of foot, except toes
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Other specified antibiotics causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

INDICATION:  History: ___ with left nephrostomy tube and drainage from tube

TECHNIQUE:  Supine AP view of the abdomen

COMPARISON:  ___ and ___

FINDINGS: 

The pigtail of the percutaneous nephroureter stent overlies the right pelvis,
in unchanged position compared to the recent fluoroscopic images from ___. Clips are seen within the right pelvis from a loop ileostomy. Bowel gas
pattern is unremarkable. Dysmorphic bony pelvis is re- demonstrated with
chronic dislocation of the left femoral head relative to the acetabulum and
diastases of the pubic symphysis. Fusion hardware within the thoracolumbar
spine is partially imaged with associated laminectomies and bone graft
material.

IMPRESSION: 

Nephroureteral stent remains in unchanged position.

EXAMINATION:  CHEST (PA AND LAT)

INDICATION:  History: ___ with chest pain

TECHNIQUE:  Upright AP and lateral views of the chest

COMPARISON:  ___

FINDINGS: 

Right-sided PICC has been removed.  Cardiac silhouette size is normal.
Mediastinal and hilar contours are unremarkable. Pulmonary vasculature is
normal. Lungs are clear. No pleural effusion or pneumothorax is present.
Posterior fusion hardware spanning the thoracolumbar spine is incompletely
imaged. Multilevel degenerative changes are noted in the thoracic spine.

IMPRESSION: 

No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with percutaneous nephrostomy, here with leaking
around tube. // eval peructaneous nephrostomy

COMPARISON:  Nephro ureteral stent exchange ___

TECHNIQUE:
OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and Dr. ___
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure. The attending,
Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the procedure. Dr. ___,
___ radiologist, personally supervised the trainee during the key
components of the procedure and reviewed and agreed with the trainee's
findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
200mcg of fentanyl and 4 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 43 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl, midazolam, lidocaine
CONTRAST: 40 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 15.9 min, 3542 cGy-cm2

PROCEDURE:  1. Left diagnostic antegrade nephrostogram.
2. Left modified 8 ___ x 22 cm nephroureteral stent exchange.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
prone on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The left flank was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Diluted contrast was injected into the left catheter to confirm current
position. The image was stored on PACS.  Local anesthesia was administered
with instillation of lidocaine jelly and 1% subcutaneous lidocaine injection.
The catheter was cut. A ___ wire was advanced into the catheter and
advanced into the ileostomy. The proximal retaining loop was unformed. The
catheter was removed over the wire. A new 8 ___ x 22 cm nephroureteral
stent was cut just proximal to the distal pigtail to prevent the catheter from
protruding out of the patient's ileostomy. The catheter was advanced over the
wire into appropriate position. The wire and stiffener were removed and the
proximal retention loop was formed. The length of the catheter was too short.
A new 8 ___ by 22 cm nephroureteral stent was cut in the middle of the
distal pigtail. The new nephroureteral stent was advanced over the wire. The
stent could not easily be advanced past a narrowing at the ureteropelvic
junction. The wire was exchanged for an Amplatz wire. An 8 ___ peel-away
sheath was advanced over the wire into the proximal ureter. The modified
nephroureteral stent was advanced over the wire. The distal end of the stent
could not be easily advanced past folds in the ileostomy. The wire was
withdrawn to form a J loop in the distal catheter which could then be advanced
further into the ileostomy. The proximal retention loop was formed and
contrast injection confirmed appropriate positioning. The final image was
saved. The catheter was then flushed. The catheter was secured with 0-silk
suture and a Stat Lock device and sterile dressings. The patient tolerated the
procedure well and there were no immediate post-procedure complications.

FINDINGS:



1. Left UPJ narrowing.
2. Distal left ureteral stricture at ileostomy anastomosis.
3. Appropriate final position of a left nephroureteral stent.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful exchange of a left nephroureteral stent for a new ___ x 22cm stent
which has been shortened to ovoid protruding through the ileostomy stoma.

conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in because of leaking around your nephrostomy tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Since they replaced the tube last time I was here, it’s been leaking through the bandage. It soaks right through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were here about a week ago for the foot infection and the tube was replaced then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. They changed it during that stay. It seemed fine at first, but then the leaking started a couple days later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. We’ll take a look. Any fever, chills, or pain in your side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. But I do have that usual flank discomfort when I take a deep breath. Nothing worse than normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And how’s your energy? You mentioned in the ED your thinking has felt a bit foggy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s been kind of cloudy. Ever since my nephrologist said I might need dialysis soon. I’ve been stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll check your labs to see if there’s anything going on with your kidneys that could be affecting your thinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my foot — it’s not infected anymore, right? I finished the antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your left foot looks clean, no redness or swelling. You’ve completed the linezolid, so we won’t continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get some urine and blood tests tonight. Your creatinine is 3.7, which is close to your baseline, so no acute kidney injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal for me. But I haven’t seen my kidney doctor in months. Missed appointments because of all these hospital stays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already called nephrology. They’ll see you tomorrow and help with next steps, including dialysis planning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back — it shows E. coli, but you’re not having symptoms like burning or urgency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, my urine seems fine. Does that mean I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since you’re not symptomatic, treating it could lead to resistance. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work also shows mild acidosis — low bicarbonate. This is common in advanced kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that what’s making my head feel foggy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We call it toxic metabolic encephalopathy — a fancy way of saying kidney changes can affect brain clarity. It should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the sodium bicarbonate help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Nephrology is increasing your dose to 1300 mg twice daily to help correct the acidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed the imaging. There’s a narrowing at the ureteropelvic junction and near the ileostomy. That might be why the tube isn’t staying sealed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s causing the leak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. Interventional radiology will replace the tube tomorrow with one better suited for the anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get light sedation — fentanyl and midazolam — so you’ll be comfortable. The team will use X-ray guidance to place it correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you just got back from the procedure. They successfully replaced the nephrostomy tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I barely felt anything. How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They found a stricture at the UPJ and near the ileostomy. The new tube was shortened so it wouldn’t poke out and now it’s seated well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And is it still leaking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the site is dry. The contrast injection confirmed good positioning and no leakage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your repeat urine culture shows no growth. The E. coli isn’t growing anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not growing now, and since you’re not symptomatic, we won’t treat it. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mental clarity is improving. You seem more alert today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel sharper. Less foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your bicarbonate is up to 20, so the increased dose is helping correct the acidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures were negative — no bloodstream infection. And your C. diff test was negative too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Glad it’s not back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple days. Your nephrostomy site is dry, labs are stable, and you’re feeling better mentally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Do I need to come back for anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have a nephrology follow-up scheduled. They’ll discuss dialysis options and monitor your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest creatinine is 3.5 — still stable. And your CBC shows mild anemia, but that’s chronic for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for years. Just need to keep taking iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, except sodium bicarbonate is now 1300 mg twice daily. Continue Keppra and tizanidine for seizures and spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue OxyContin and Percocet as needed. Watch for constipation — keep using docusate and senna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check — your nephrostomy site is dry, no signs of infection. You’re ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. No more leaking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None seen since the tube was replaced. Keep the site clean and dry, and call if it starts leaking again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have nephrology in one week. They’ll help you prepare for dialysis when the time comes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about that, but I know it’s coming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll guide you through it. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you’re being discharged home today. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing will go over your discharge instructions and medications one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your mental status is much better. The encephalopathy has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like myself again. Thanks for figuring it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for evaluation of leaking from his left nephrostomy tube, which began after a recent replacement during a prior hospitalization. He has a complex medical history including T12 paraplegia, chronic kidney disease stage IV, neurogenic bladder, and recurrent urinary infections. Imaging revealed a stricture at the ureteropelvic junction and near the ileostomy anastomosis, contributing to the leakage. The nephrostomy tube was successfully exchanged with a modified stent, resolving the leak. He was found to have asymptomatic bacteriuria with E. coli, which did not require treatment. His chronic metabolic acidosis improved with an increased dose of sodium bicarbonate, and his previously noted toxic metabolic encephalopathy resolved. Nephrology was consulted, and a follow-up appointment was scheduled to discuss future dialysis planning. He remained stable, with no signs of active infection or complications, and was discharged home in improved condition.
